strong: City of Milpitas Local Funding Measure.

text: Shall an ordinance to update City of Milpitas's 50-year-old business tax be adopted, with no tax increase to residents, so small businesses pay less than larger businesses, with all paying an annual flat rate, plus 0.025% to 0.035% of gross receipts for larger businesses, providing approximately $3,000,000 annually for general city services such as maintaining fiscal stability, neighborhood safety/cleanliness; requiring public disclosure, all funds invested locally, until ended by voters?
A "yes" vote adopts the new gross receipts business tax to replace the existing tax.
A "no" vote rejects the new gross receipts business tax and keeps the existing tax.
Measure K seeks voter approval of an ordinance that replaces the City's current business tax with a new tax based on gross receipts.

Currently, the City's uses a business tax formula that was adopted in 1976. It requires each business to pay an amount based on its relevant industry (e.g. "retail," "manufacturing," "beauty salon," etc.) and its number of employees. Neither the rates nor the categories of businesses have been updated since.

The proposed ordinance would replace the existing per-employee formula with a gross receipts model. Each business would pay a tax based on the gross receipts it earned from operating in Milpitas. Gross receipts (as defined in the ordinance) include all money that a business takes in, without deducting expenses. It does not include things like refunds or deposits that the business does not earn.

The table below shows the formula for the new tax. Each business would pay a flat rate ranging from $25 to $400 based on the tier in which its gross receipts fall. Additionally, businesses making more than $700,000 would pay a rate ranging from 0.025% to 0.035% of that portion of their gross receipts falling in the top three tiers. The flat rate would increase automatically each year with inflation.

The ordinance also includes provisions governing the administration of the tax, including processes for annual collection, delinquencies, penalties and interest, appeals and refunds, inspection and audit, and enforcement. It specifies certain businesses, like non-profits, that are exempt from the tax. If approved, the new tax would go into effect January 1, 2028.

Proceeds of the new tax would continue to be (i) deposited in the City's general fund, (ii) annually audited and publicly reported in the City's annual audit, and (iii) available for any lawful municipal purpose. Most services provided by the City, such as police/fire/ambulance services, street and sidewalk repair services, and park and recreation services, are funded from the general fund. The general fund budget, and expenditures from the general fund, are controlled locally by the Milpitas City Council.
This measure was placed on the ballot by the City Council of the City of Milpitas.

The above statement is an impartial analysis of Measure K. If you desire a copy of the measure, please call the elections official's office at 408.586.3005 and a copy will be mailed at no cost to you.

/s/ Christian M. Curtis
City Attorney

strong: Measure K does not raise taxes for residents or homeowners.

text: Right now, small and locally owned businesses have a higher tax rate than larger, wealthier corporations—in some cases, over 70 times more.
This is simply not fair! And we have the power to make it right.

strong: Voting Yes on K fixes this inequity by ensuring large corporations finally pay their fair share for the essential services we all rely on.

text: Yes on K reforms our business tax structure that's over 50 years old to make it fair for small business, while providing our community with local funding to maintain our quality of life—without raising taxes for residents.
Yes on K maintains our vital city services and fiscal stability.
Yes on K maintains emergency medical and ambulance services.
Yes on K replaces aging water and sewer lines, and repairs storm drains.
Yes on K keeps neighborhood streets and sidewalks clean and well-maintained and removes blight and illegal dumping.
With Washington and Sacramento politicians cutting funding for our city, our critical services—including 911 emergency response and street repair—are at stake.
That's why it's more important than ever that we remain self-reliant.

em: Apparently, out-of-town Special Interest groups either haven't done their homework, or worse—don't want large corporations to pay their fair share! Reject their lies—vote YES on K.
Milpitas's small, locally owned businesses shouldn't be stuck with a higher tax rate than Big Corporations. While opponents play politics, YES on K provides a solution to an unfair tax system.
FACT: Measure K simply reforms an outdated, 50-year-old business tax structure.

FACT: Currently, some Milpitas small businesses pay 70 times higher in business tax per employee than Big Corporations! Measure K fixes this inequity, so corporations pay their fair share for the services we ALL use.
FACT: Measure K lowers taxes for the smallest businesses.

strong: FACT: Measure K does NOT raise taxes on residents and homeowners.

em: Measure K was developed with the input of small businesses to reform a structure currently unfair to them.
Large corporations use 911 and Milpitas streets just like us. Yet Milpitas residents and small businesses are shouldering an unfair share of costs for these services.
It's time we ask Big Business to pay their fair share!

Measure K is fiscally accountable and transparent to our residents and business community. Every dollar must be reinvested locally and is subject to independent audits and public disclosure of all spending.
Reject political rhetoric, support Milpitas's small businesses, and maintain the quality of life for Milpitas families during these tough times.
To read official Measure K information: www.Milpitas.gov.
